paragraphs: Extras are people in the background of films and TV shows. The Extras Department is a big agency for extras. It is based in Belfast.
The agency has more than 20,000 members. It works for big companies like HBO, the BBC and RTÉ.
Now it will stop working in the Republic of Ireland. It told its members by email on Tuesday.
The reason is a new UK law. Before a job starts, companies must check that each worker is allowed to work in the UK. Many extras work for just one day, so this is a lot of extra work.
Members in the Republic can still work in Northern Ireland if they pass the check. But the trip can be expensive.

paragraphs: The Extras Department, one of the biggest agencies for film and TV extras on the island of Ireland, is stopping its work in the Republic. The agency is based in Belfast and told members in the Republic by email on Tuesday.
The agency has more than 20,000 extras and stand-ins on its books. Its clients include HBO, Universal, RTÉ and the BBC. Its website had said that a Dublin office would open soon.

The agency said the reason is a UK law called Right to Work. Under this law, companies must check that a person is allowed to work in the UK before the job begins. Since 1 October, the rule also covers contractors. Because many extras only work for one day, the checks have created a lot of paperwork.

Members in the Republic who already have the right to work in the UK can still take jobs in Northern Ireland, although travel may be expensive. To stay with the agency, they must show ID to an outside company and then have a video call with the agency.

paragraphs: The Extras Department, a Belfast-based agency that supplies extras for film and television across the island, is ending its operations in the Republic of Ireland. It informed members there in an email on Tuesday.

The agency, which has been the only large-scale business of its kind in Northern Ireland since 2007, has more than 20,000 extras, featured extras and stand-ins on its books. Its clients include HBO, Universal, RTÉ and the BBC, and its website had previously advertised the upcoming launch of a Dublin office.

The agency blamed the UK's Right to Work legislation, which has significantly increased its administrative workload. The law requires businesses to verify that a person is legally entitled to work before a job begins, and on 1 October the requirement was extended to contractors and directly engaged workers. Since many extras work for only a single day, compliance has proved difficult.

Members based in the Republic who already hold the right to work in the UK can still accept bookings in Northern Ireland, although travel costs may be high. To remain on the books, they must complete an identity check through an external provider, followed by a video call with the agency.
